claim: For small perturbations, the active response of muscle is well captured by a linear-time-invariant (LTI) system: a stiff spring in parallel with a light damper.
source: For small perturbations, the active response of muscle is well captured by a linear-time-invariant (LTI) system: a stiff spring in parallel with a light damper.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 1994 experiments described later in the text, and represents an established finding in the field.

claim: The force response of muscle to longer stretches is better represented by a compliant spring that can fix its end when activated.
source: The force response of muscle to longer stretches is better represented by a compliant spring that can fix its end when activated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental work referenced in the abstract and detailed later with citations to Herzog and Leonard, 2002 and Leonard et al., 2010.

claim: The stiffness and damping (impedance) of muscle in response to small perturbations is of fundamental importance to motor learning and mechanical stability.
source: Experimental work has shown that the stiffness and damping (impedance) of muscle in response to small perturbations is of fundamental importance to motor learning and mechanical stability
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work on motor learning and stability.

claim: The huge forces developed during long active stretches are critical for simulating and predicting injury.
source: while the huge forces developed during long active stretches are critical for simulating and predicting injury.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact based on experimental work.

claim: Muscle is actively lengthened as a part of nearly all terrestrial locomotion.
source: Outside of motor learning and injury, muscle is actively lengthened as a part of nearly all terrestrial locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about muscle function during locomotion.

claim: No single muscle model has all the mechanical properties needed to capture impedance and active lengthening.
source: Despite the functional importance of impedance and active lengthening, no single muscle model has all these mechanical properties.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that motivates the current work.

claim: The VEXAT model can replicate the response of muscle to length changes great and small.
source: In this work, we present the viscoelastic-crossbridge active-titin (VEXAT) model that can replicate the response of muscle to length changes great and small.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by simulations and comparisons presented throughout.

claim: The VEXAT model more accurately captures the impedance of biological muscle and its responses to long active stretches than a Hill-type model.
source: The VEXAT model more accurately captures the impedance of biological muscle and its responses to long active stretches than a Hill-type model and can still reproduce the force-velocity and force-length relations of muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative simulations presented in the results section.

claim: The VEXAT model can reproduce the force-velocity and force-length relations of muscle.
source: The VEXAT model more accurately captures the impedance of biological muscle and its responses to long active stretches than a Hill-type model and can still reproduce the force-velocity and force-length relations of muscle.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations of Hill, 1938 and Gordon et al., 1966 experiments.

claim: The low frequency phase response of the VEXAT model can be improved.
source: While the comparison between the VEXAT model and biological muscle is favorable, there are some phenomena that can be improved: the low frequency phase response of the model, and a mechanism to support passive force enhancement.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation based on comparison with experimental data.

claim: The VEXAT model lacks a mechanism to support passive force enhancement.
source: While the comparison between the VEXAT model and biological muscle is favorable, there are some phenomena that can be improved: the low frequency phase response of the model, and a mechanism to support passive force enhancement.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation based on comparison with experimental data showing passive force enhancement.

claim: The CNS exploits the activation-dependent stiffness and damping (impedance) of muscle when learning new movements.
source: The CNS exploits the activation-dependent stiffness and damping (impedance) of muscle when learning new movements (Franklin et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franklin et al., 2003.

claim: The CNS uses muscle impedance when moving in unstable or noisy environments.
source: The CNS exploits the activation-dependent stiffness and damping (impedance) of muscle when learning new movements (Franklin et al., 2003), and when moving in unstable (Trumbower et al., 2009) or noisy environments (Selen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Trumbower et al., 2009 and Selen et al., 2009.

claim: The CNS uses co-contraction to increase the stiffness of the arm when perturbed by an unstable force field.
source: Reaching experiments using haptic manipulanda show that the CNS uses co-contraction to increase the stiffness of the arm when perturbed by an unstable force field (Burdet et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burdet et al., 2001.

claim: With time and repetition, the force field becomes learned and co-contraction is reduced.
source: With time and repetition, the force field becomes learned and co-contraction is reduced (Franklin et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franklin et al., 2003.

claim: Kirsch et al., 1994 showed that muscle behaves like a linear-time-invariant (LTI) system in response to small perturbations.
source: Under constant activation and at a consistent nominal length, Kirsch et al., 1994 were able to show that muscle behaves like a linear-time-invariant (LTI) system in response to small perturbations (see Appendix 9, Note 1)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: A spring-damper of best fit captured over 90% of the observed variation in muscle force for small perturbations (1–3.8% optimal length) over a wide range of bandwidths (4–90 Hz).
source: a spring-damper of best fit captured over 90% of the observed variation in muscle force for small perturbations (1–3.8% optimal length) over a wide range of bandwidths (4–90 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 1994 data.

claim: When active muscle is stretched appreciably, titin can develop enormous forces.
source: When active muscle is stretched appreciably, titin can develop enormous forces (Herzog and Leonard, 2002; Leonard et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Herzog and Leonard, 2002 and Leonard et al., 2010.

claim: Titin may prevent further lengthening and injury when active muscle is stretched appreciably.
source: When active muscle is stretched appreciably, titin can develop enormous forces (Herzog and Leonard, 2002; Leonard et al., 2010), which may prevent further lengthening and injury.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observation that titin develops large forces during stretching.

claim: The stiffness that best captures the response of muscle to small perturbations is far greater than the stiffness that best captures the response of muscle to large perturbations.
source: The stiffness that best captures the response of muscle to the small perturbations of Kirsch et al., 1994 is far greater than the stiffness that best captures the response of muscle to large perturbations (Herzog and Leonard, 2002; Leonard et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing data from Kirsch et al., 1994 with Herzog and Leonard, 2002 and Leonard et al., 2010.

claim: Everyday movements are often accompanied by both large and small kinematic perturbations.
source: Since everyday movements are often accompanied by both large and small kinematic perturbations, it is important to accurately capture these two processes.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about movement.

claim: There is likely no single muscle model that can replicate the force response of muscle to small and large perturbations while also retaining the capability to reproduce the experiments of Hill, 1938 and Gordon et al., 1966.
source: However, there is likely no single muscle model that can replicate the force response of muscle to small (Kirsch et al., 1994) and large perturbations (Herzog and Leonard, 2002; Leonard et al., 2010) while also retaining the capability to reproduce the experiments of Hill, 1938 and Gordon et al., 1966.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature based on inference from existing models.

claim: Simulation studies that depend on an accurate replication of the perturbation response may reach conclusions well justified in simulation but not in reality.
source: Unfortunately, this means that simulation studies that depend on an accurate replication of the perturbation response may reach conclusions well justified in simulation but not in reality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of existing models.

claim: Hill-type muscle models do not contain any active spring elements.
source: Neither Hill nor Huxley models are likely to replicate the experiments of Kirsch et al., 1994 because a Hill muscle model (Zajac, 1989; Millard et al., 2013) does not contain any active spring elements
evidence: This is stated as a known property of Hill-type models with citations.

claim: Huxley models lack an active damping element.
source: while a Huxley model lacks an active damping element.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of Huxley models.

claim: Linearized muscle models can replicate the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994.
source: Although linearized muscle models can replicate the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994, these models are only accurate for small changes in length
evidence: This is stated based on the properties of linearized models.

claim: Linearized muscle models cannot replicate the nonlinear force-velocity relation of Hill, 1938, nor the nonlinear force-length relation of Gordon et al., 1966.
source: these models are only accurate for small changes in length and cannot replicate the nonlinear force-velocity relation of Hill, 1938, nor the nonlinear force-length relation of Gordon et al., 1966.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of linearized models.

claim: The model of Forcinito et al., 1998 more faithfully replicates the force development of active muscle during ramp length changes compared to a Hill-type model.
source: This modification allows the model of Forcinito et al., 1998 to more faithfully replicate the force development of active muscle, as compared to a Hill-type model, during ramp length changes of ≈10% (see Appendix 9, Note 4) of the optimal CE length, and across velocities of 4–11% of the maximum contraction velocity (see Appendix 9, Note 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Forcinito et al., 1998.

claim: The model of Tamura and Saito, 2002 replicated the force-length-velocity relations as well as qualitatively reproducing the force and stiffness profiles of force-enhancement and force-depression.
source: By carefully selecting the dynamics that drive the two elements, the model of Tamura and Saito, 2002 replicated the force-length-velocity relations (Gordon et al., 1966; Hill, 1938) as well as qualitatively reproducing the force and stiffness profiles (Tamura et al., 2005) of force-enhancement and force-depression as measured by Sugi and Tsuchiya, 1988.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tamura and Saito, 2002 and Tamura et al., 2005.

claim: The models of Forcinito et al., 1998, Tamura and Saito, 2002, Haeufle et al., 2014, and Günther et al., 2018 are unlikely to reproduce the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because their linearized versions lead to a serial connection of a spring and a damper.
source: While each of these models improves upon the force response of the Hill model to ramp length changes, none are likely to reproduce the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because the linearized versions of these models lead to a serial, rather than a parallel, connection of a spring and a damper
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of these models and the requirements shown by Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: Kirsch et al., 1994 specifically showed that a serial connection of a spring-damper fails to reproduce the phase shift between force and length present in their experimental data.
source: Kirsch et al., 1994 specifically showed (see Figure 3 of Kirsch et al., 1994) that a serial connection of a spring-damper fails to reproduce the phase shift between force and length present in their experimental data.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: Titin is a gigantic multi-segmented protein that spans a half-sarcomere, attaching to the Z-line at one end and the middle of the thick filament at the other end.
source: Titin is a gigantic multi-segmented protein that spans a half-sarcomere, attaching to the Z-line at one end and the middle of the thick filament at the other end (Maruyama et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maruyama et al., 1985.

claim: In skeletal muscle, the proximal immunoglobulin (IgP) segment and the PEVK segment are the most compliant sections of titin.
source: In skeletal muscle, the two sections nearest to the Z-line, the proximal immunoglobulin (IgP) segment and the PEVK segment — rich in the amino acids proline (P), glutamate (E), valine (V) and lysine (K) — are the most compliant (Trombitás et al., 1998b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Trombitás et al., 1998b.

claim: The distal immunoglobulin (IgD) segments bind strongly to the thick filament.
source: since the distal immunoglobulin (IgD) segments bind strongly to the thick filament (Houmeida et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Houmeida et al., 1995.

claim: Titin varies in composition and geometry between different muscle types.
source: Titin has proven to be a complex filament, varying in composition and geometry between different muscle types (Tomalka et al., 2019; Boldt et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tomalka et al., 2019 and Boldt et al., 2020.

claim: Titin varies widely between species.
source: widely between species (Lindstedt and Nishikawa, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lindstedt and Nishikawa, 2017.

claim: Titin can apply activation dependent forces to actin.
source: and can apply activation dependent forces to actin (Kellermayer and Granzier, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kellermayer and Granzier, 1996.

claim: Experimental observations have reported titin-actin interactions at myosin-actin binding sites.
source: Experimental observations have reported titin-actin interactions at myosin-actin binding sites (Astier et al., 1998; Niederländer et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Astier et al., 1998 and Niederländer et al., 2004.

claim: Experimental observations have reported interactions between titin's PEVK region and actin.
source: between titin's PEVK region and actin (Bianco et al., 2007; Nagy et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bianco et al., 2007 and Nagy et al., 2004.

claim: Experimental observations have reported interactions between titin's N2A region and actin.
source: between titin's N2A region and actin (Dutta et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dutta et al., 2018.

claim: Experimental observations have reported interactions between the PEVK-IgD regions of titin and myosin.
source: and between the PEVK-IgD regions of titin and myosin (DuVall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to DuVall et al., 2017.

claim: Most motor control simulations make use of the canonical linearized muscle model.
source: Although most motor control simulations (Kearney et al., 1997; Perreault et al., 2004; Schouten et al., 2008; Trumbower et al., 2009; Mitrovic et al., 2010) make use of the canonical linearized muscle model
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to motor control simulation studies.

claim: At the optimal CE length, the approach of Sartori et al., 2015 would predict an active muscle stiffness of zero since the slope of the force-length curve is zero.
source: at the optimal CE length this approach would predict an active muscle stiffness of zero since the slope of the force-length curve is zero
evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical properties of the approach described by Sartori et al., 2015.

claim: On the descending limb, the approach of Sartori et al., 2015 would predict a negative active muscle stiffness since the slope of the force-length curve is negative.
source: on the descending limb this approach would predict a negative active muscle stiffness since the slope of the force-length curve is negative.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical properties of the approach described by Sartori et al., 2015.

claim: CE stiffness is large and positive near the optimal length.
source: In contrast, CE stiffness is large and positive near the optimal length (Kirsch et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: There is no evidence for negative stiffness on the descending limb of the force-length curve.
source: and there is no evidence for negative stiffness on the descending limb of the force-length curve (Herzog and Leonard, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Herzog and Leonard, 2002.

claim: De Groote et al., 2017 and De Groote et al., 2018 modeled short-range-stiffness using a stiff spring in parallel with the active force element of a Hill-type muscle model.
source: In contrast, De Groote et al., 2017 and De Groote et al., 2018 modeled short-range-stiffness using a stiff spring in parallel with the active force element of a Hill-type muscle model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Groote et al., 2017 and De Groote et al., 2018.

claim: The short-range-stiffness of the muscle sharply goes to zero outside of the specified range in the De Groote et al., 2017 and De Groote et al., 2018 model, whereas in reality the stiffness is only reduced.
source: the short-range-stiffness of the muscle sharply goes to zero outside of the specified range whereas in reality the stiffness is only reduced (Kirsch et al., 1994, see Figure 9A)
evidence: This is a critique based on comparison with data from Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: The damping of the canonical Hill-model likely differs substantially from biological muscle.
source: the damping of the canonical Hill-model has been left unchanged and likely differs substantially from biological muscle (Kirsch et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with data from Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: The VEXAT model can capture the force development of muscle to perturbations that vary in size and timescale.
source: In this work, we propose a model that can capture the force development of muscle to perturbations that vary in size and timescale
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by simulations presented in the results.

claim: The VEXAT model is described using only a few states making it well suited for large-scale simulations.
source: and yet is described using only a few states making it well suited for large-scale simulations.
evidence: This is stated as a design goal and property of the model.

claim: The assumption that mechanical properties scale with size is commonly used when modeling muscle.
source: The assumption that mechanical properties scale with size is commonly used when modeling muscle (Zajac, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zajac, 1989.

claim: Titin's passive-force-length properties scale from single molecules to myofibrils.
source: and titin's passive-force-length properties scale from single molecules to myofibrils (Herzog et al., 2012; Prado et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Herzog et al., 2012 and Prado et al., 2005.

claim: The stiffness of actin and myosin filaments greatly exceeds that of crossbridges.
source: since the stiffness of actin (Higuchi et al., 1995) and myosin filaments (Tajima et al., 1994) greatly exceeds that of crossbridges (Veigel et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Higuchi et al., 1995, Tajima et al., 1994, and Veigel et al., 1998.

claim: Actin and myosin filaments are treated as rigid in the VEXAT model.
source: we treat actin and myosin filaments as rigid to reduce the number of states needed to simulate this model.
evidence: This is stated as a modeling assumption to reduce computational complexity.

claim: The VEXAT model lumps the six titin filaments per half-sarcomere together.
source: Similarly, we have lumped the six titin filaments per half-sarcomere (Figure 1A) together to further reduce the number of states needed to simulate this model.
evidence: This is stated as a modeling decision and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There is evidence for a titin-actin interaction near titin's N2A region.
source: While there is evidence for titin-actin interaction near titin's N2A region (Dutta et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dutta et al., 2018.

claim: There is support for a titin-actin interaction occurring near titin's PEVK region.
source: there is also support for a titin-actin interaction occurring near titin's PEVK region (Bianco et al., 2007; Nagy et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bianco et al., 2007 and Nagy et al., 2004.

claim: There is support for a titin-myosin interaction near the PEVK-IgD region.
source: and for a titin-myosin interaction near the PEVK-IgD region (DuVall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to DuVall et al., 2017.

claim: Current evidence weighs more heavily towards a titin-actin interaction than a titin-myosin interaction.
source: For the purposes of our model, we will assume a titin-actin interaction because current evidence weighs more heavily towards a titin-actin interaction than a titin-myosin interaction.
evidence: This is stated as a justification for the modeling choice based on the weight of evidence.

claim: The titin-actin interaction is not a rigid attachment, but instead is an activation dependent damping.
source: Here, we assume that this interaction is not a rigid attachment, but instead is an activation dependent damping to be consistent with the observations of Kellermayer and Granzier, 1996 and Dutta et al., 2018
evidence: This is stated as a modeling assumption based on experimental observations.

claim: Adding titin filaments and calcium slowed, but did not stop, the progression of actin filaments across a plate covered in active crossbridges.
source: adding titin filaments and calcium slowed, but did not stop, the progression of actin filaments across a plate covered in active crossbridges (an in vitro motility assay).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from Kellermayer and Granzier, 1996 and Dutta et al., 2018.

claim: Kirsch et al., 1994 used system identification methods to identify LTI mechanical systems that best describes how muscle transforms input length waveforms to output force waveforms.
source: Kirsch et al., 1994 used system identification methods to identify LTI mechanical systems that best describes how muscle transforms input length waveforms to output force waveforms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: The damping coefficient of best fit increases as the bandwidth of the perturbation decreases.
source: Kirsch et al., 1994 repeated the experiment using perturbations that had a variety of lengths (0.4 mm, 0.8 mm, and 1.6 mm) and bandwidths (15 Hz, 35 Hz, and 90 Hz) and observed a peculiar quality of muscle: the damping coefficient of best fit increases as the bandwidth of the perturbation decreases (see Figures 3 and 10 of Kirsch et al., 1994 for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: When coupled with an elastic-tendon, neither the VEXAT model nor the Hill model can match the VAF of the analysis of Kirsch et al., 1994 for 15 Hz perturbations.
source: When coupled with an elastic-tendon, the 15 Hz perturbations show that neither model can match the VAF of the analysis of Kirsch et al., 1994 (compare Figure 6A to G)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At 90 Hz the VEXAT model reaches a VAF of 89% which is within the range of 78–99% reported by Kirsch et al., 1994.
source: while at 90 Hz the VEXAT model reaches a VAF of 89% (Figure 6D) which is within the range of 78–99% reported by Kirsch et al., 1994.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The Hill model's VAF at 90 Hz remains low at 58%.
source: In contrast, the Hill model's VAF at 90 Hz remains low at 58% (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Both the VEXAT and Hill models have a greater phase shift than the data of Kirsch et al., 1994 at low frequencies.
source: both models have a greater phase shift than the data of Kirsch et al., 1994 at low frequencies (compare Figure 6C to I and F to L).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The experiment of Herzog and Leonard, 2002 is important for showing that biological muscle does not exhibit negative stiffness on the descending limb of the active-force-length curve.
source: The experiment of Herzog and Leonard, 2002 is important for showing that biological muscle does not exhibit negative stiffness on the descending limb of the active-force-length curve.
evidence: This is stated as the significance of the Herzog and Leonard, 2002 experiment.

claim: After the initial transient, the VEXAT model continues to develop increased tension as it is lengthened, while the Hill model's tension drops before recovering.
source: After the initial force transient, the response of the two models diverges (Figure 9B): the VEXAT model continues to develop increased tension as it is lengthened, while the Hill model's tension drops before recovering.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The Hill model develops less force during lengthening when it enters a small region of negative stiffness.
source: In contrast, the Hill model develops less force during lengthening when it enters a small region of negative stiffness (Figure 9B and C)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 9B and C.

claim: Leonard et al., 2010 recorded active forces both within and far beyond actin-myosin overlap.
source: The active-lengthening experiment of Leonard et al., 2010 provides some insight into this force distribution problem because they recorded active forces both within and far beyond actin-myosin overlap.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leonard et al., 2010.

claim: The data of Leonard et al., 2010 shows that active force continues to develop linearly during lengthening, beyond actin-myosin overlap, until mechanical failure.
source: The data of Leonard et al., 2010 shows that active force continues to develop linearly during lengthening, beyond actin-myosin overlap, until mechanical failure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leonard et al., 2010.

claim: Leonard et al., 2010 showed that titin-deleted myofibrils failed at short lengths and insignificant stresses.
source: To show that the extraordinary forces beyond actin-myosin overlap can be ascribed to titin, Leonard et al., 2010 repeated the experiment but deleted titin using trypsin: the titin-deleted myoﬁbrils failed at short lengths and insigniﬁcant stresses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leonard et al., 2010.

claim: When the slow active stretch of the experiment of Leonard et al., 2010 is simulated, only the VEXAT model with the linear titin element can match the experimental data.
source: When the slow active stretch (0.1 µm/sarcomere/s) of the experiment of Leonard et al., 2010 is simulated, only the VEXAT model with the linear titin element can match the experimental data of Leonard et al., 2010 (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The maximum shortening velocity of the VEXAT model is slightly weaker than the embedded curve due to the series viscoelasticity of the XE element.
source: The maximum shortening velocity of the VEXAT model is slightly weaker than the embedded curve due to the series viscoelasticity of the XE element.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model structure and simulation results.

claim: The VEXAT model produces a force-length profile that is shifted to the right of the Hill model due to the series elasticity introduced by the XE.
source: The simulation of Gordon et al., 1966 shows that the VEXAT model (Figure 12A, blue dots) produces a force-length proﬁle that is shifted to the right of the Hill model (Figure 12A, red line) due to the series elasticity introduced by the XE.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 12A.

claim: The origins of the activation-dependent damping observed by Kirsch et al., 1994 have not yet been established.
source: While there is evidence that the activation-dependent stiffness of muscle originates primarily from the stiffness of the attached crossbridges (Veigel et al., 1998), the origins of the activation-dependent damping observed by Kirsch et al., 1994 have not yet been established.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field.

claim: The VEXAT model assumes that the damping originates from the attached crossbridges since the damping observed by Kirsch et al., 1994 varies linearly with activation.
source: We assumed that, since the damping observed by Kirsch et al., 1994 varies linearly with activation, the damping originates from the attached crossbridges.
evidence: This is stated as a modeling assumption based on experimental observations.

claim: A recent experiment suggests the force developed by the XE might decrease during lengthening rather than increasing as is typical of a Hill model.
source: A recent experiment (see Figure 7 of Tomalka et al., 2021) suggests the force developed by the XE might decrease during lengthening rather than increasing as is typical of a Hill model (Millard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tomalka et al., 2021.

claim: If the observations of Tomalka et al., 2021 can be replicated, the VEXAT model will need to be adjusted.
source: If the observations of Tomalka et al., 2021 can be replicated, the VEXAT model will need to be adjusted so that the XE element develops less force during active lengthening while the active-titin element develops more force.
evidence: This is stated as a potential future modification based on new experimental evidence.

claim: The VEXAT model assumes that actin-myosin sliding acceleration occurs when there is a force imbalance between the external force applied to the XE and the internal force developed by the XE.
source: Finally, we have assumed that actin-myosin sliding acceleration (due to crossbridge cycling) occurs when there is a force imbalance between the external force applied to the XE and the internal force developed by the XE as shown in Equation 16.
evidence: This is stated as a modeling assumption.

claim: Hill-type models assume that the tension applied to the muscle instantaneously affects the actin-myosin sliding velocity.
source: This assumption is a departure from previous models: Hill-type models (Zajac, 1989; Millard et al., 2013) assume that the tension applied to the muscle instantaneously affects the actin-myosin sliding velocity
evidence: This is stated as a known property of Hill-type models with citations.

claim: Huxley models assume that the actin-myosin sliding velocity directly affects the rate of attachment and detachment of crossbridges.
source: Huxley models (Huxley, 1957) assume that the actin-myosin sliding velocity directly affects the rate of attachment and detachment of crossbridges.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of Huxley models with citation.

claim: The active titin model assumes that some parts of the PEVK segment bond to actin, and this bond cannot do any positive work on titin.
source: The active titin model that we have developed makes assumptions similar to Rode et al., 2009 and Schappacher-Tilp et al., 2015: some parts of the PEVK segment bond to actin, and this bond cannot do any positive work on titin.
evidence: This is stated as a modeling assumption similar to previous models.

claim: The assumption that the bond between titin and actin cannot do positive work means that titin cannot be actively preloaded.
source: The assumption that the bond between titin and actin cannot do positive work means that titin cannot be actively preloaded: it can only develop force when it is stretched.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling assumption.

claim: If titin were significantly preloaded by crossbridge cycling, the titin load path would support higher forces and the myosin-actin load path would bear less force.
source: If titin were signiﬁcantly preloaded by crossbridge cycling, the titin load path would support higher forces and the myosin-actin load path would bear less force.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the consequences of an alternative mechanism.

claim: The XE model's output will be inaccurate when only a single crossbridge remains because it can only generate force continuously while a real crossbridge generates force discretely.
source: When only a single crossbridge remains, the XE model's output will be inaccurate because it can only generate force continuously while a real crossbridge generates force discretely each time it attaches to, and detaches from, actin.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the lumped crossbridge approach.

claim: Myosin-actin interactions and some titin-actin interactions are temperature-sensitive.
source: In contrast, myosin-actin interactions and some titin-actin interactions are temperature-sensitive (Minajeva et al., 2002; Roots et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Minajeva et al., 2002 and Roots et al., 2012.

claim: The VEXAT model in its current form ignores phenomena related to submaximal contractions.
source: Finally, the VEXAT model in its current form ignores phenomena related to submaximal contractions: the shift in the peak of the force-length relation (Stephenson and Wendt, 1984), and the scaling of the maximum shortening velocity (Chow and Darling, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current model with citations.

claim: A Huxley model is likely to have difficulty reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because the model lacks an active damping element.
source: In contrast, we have shown in the 'Biological benchmark simulations' section that a Hill-type model compares poorly to biological muscle when the same set of experiments are simulated. We expect that a Huxley model (Huxley, 1957) is also likely to have difficulty reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because the model lacks an active damping element.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of Huxley models.

claim: A Huxley model will be unable to replicate any experiment that is strongly influenced by titin such as the experiment of Leonard et al., 2010.
source: Since titin was discovered (Maruyama, 1976) long after Huxley's model was proposed (Huxley, 1957), a Huxley model will be unable to replicate any experiment that is strongly inﬂuenced by titin such as the experiment of Leonard et al., 2010.
evidence: This is an inference based on the historical development of models and the absence of titin in Huxley models.

claim: Linearized impedance models can reproduce the experiments of Kirsch et al., 1994, but these models lack the nonlinear components needed to reproduce the force-length experiments of Gordon et al., 1966, and the force-velocity experiments of Hill, 1938.
source: Linearized impedance models (Hogan, 1985; Mussa-Ivaldi et al., 1985) can reproduce the experiments of Kirsch et al., 1994, but these models lack the nonlinear components needed to reproduce the force-length experiments of Gordon et al., 1966, and the force-velocity experiments of Hill, 1938.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of linearized models with citations.

claim: At high frequencies the lack of damping in the tendon will drive the phase shift between length and force to approach zero in models with a structure that places a contractile element in series with an elastic-tendon.
source: The models of Forcinito et al., 1998, and Tahir et al., 2018 have a structure that places a contractile element in series with an elastic-tendon. While this is a commonly used structure, at high frequencies the lack of damping in the tendon will drive the phase shift between length and force to approach zero.
evidence: This is an inference based on the impedance properties of series connections.

claim: The measurements and model of Kirsch et al., 1994 indicate that the phase shift between length and force approaches ninety degrees with increasing frequencies.
source: The measurements and model of Kirsch et al., 1994, in contrast, indicate that the phase shift between length and force approaches ninety degrees with increasing frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: It is likely that models of Haeufle et al., 2014 and Günther et al., 2018 will not be able to match the frequency response of biological muscle.
source: Although the Hill-type models of Haeufle et al., 2014 and Günther et al., 2018 have viscoelastic tendons, these models have no representation of the viscoelasticity of the CE's attached crossbridges. Similar to the Hill-type muscle model evaluated in this work (Millard et al., 2013), it is likely that models of Haeufle et al., 2014 and Günther et al., 2018 will not be able to match the frequency response of biological muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of these models and comparison with the Hill model results.

claim: It is unlikely that the model of Tamura and Saito, 2002 will be able to reproduce the frequency response of biological muscle because it uses spring-damping elements in series.
source: While the model of Tamura and Saito, 2002 is one of the few models that can develop force-enhancement and force-depression (Tamura et al., 2005), it is unlikely that this model will be able to reproduce the frequency response of biological muscle because it uses spring-damping elements in series: Kirsch et al., 1994 showed that the frequency response of spring-damping elements in series poorly fits the response of biological muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of the model and data from Kirsch et al., 1994.

claim: It is unlikely that the models of De Groote et al., 2017 and De Groote et al., 2018 will reproduce the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because a Hill model has a frequency response that differs from biological muscle.
source: While the formulations presented in De Groote et al., 2017 and De Groote et al., 2018 improves upon a Hill model it is unlikely to reproduce the experiement of Kirsch et al., 1994 because we have shown in the 'Active lengthening beyond actin-myosin overlap' section that a Hill model has a frequency response that differs from biological muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results presented in the paper.

claim: The muscle model of Rode et al., 2009 uses a Hill model for the CE and so is expected to have the same difficulties reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994.
source: The muscle model of Rode et al., 2009 uses a Hill model for the CE and so we expect that this model will have the same difficulties reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of the Rode et al., 2009 model.

claim: The model of Schappacher-Tilp et al., 2015 will likely have difficulty reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because it is missing an active damping element.
source: Similar to a Huxley model, the model of Schappacher-Tilp et al., 2015 will likely have difficulty reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because it is missing an active damping element.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of the Schappacher-Tilp et al., 2015 model.
